title: Tail questions: ...isn't it? / ...do you? / ...haven't they?
shortExplanation: It's cold, isn't it? You like jazz, don't you?
longExplanation:
Tag questions are used to confirm or clarify.
Rule: affirmative sentence → negative tag, and vice versa.
Auxiliary verb in the tail = tense of the main sentence.
Intonation: ↘ (falling) = confirmation; ↗ (rising) = real question.
formation: It's cold, isn't it? You like jazz, don't you?

examples.sentence: It's a nice day, isn't it?
You don't like horror films, do you?
examples.translation: You don't like horror films, do you?

examples.sentence: She can swim, can't she?

title: have got - possession (British version)
shortExplanation: I've got a car. Have you got a pen? She hasn't got time.
longExplanation:
have got is a colloquial British form of possession. Value = have.
• Affirmation: I have got / I've got a laptop.
• Denial: I haven't got / I don't have
• Question: Have you got...? / Do you have...?
formation: I've got a car. Have you got a pen? She hasn't got time.

examples.sentence: I've got two brothers.
Have you got the time?
examples.translation: Don't you know what time it is?

examples.sentence: She hasn't got any cash.

title: Adverbs of manner: quickly, carefully, well, hard, fast
shortExplanation: She sings beautifully. He works hard. She drives fast.
longExplanation:
Most adverbs are formed from adjectives + -ly: quick → quickly, careful → carefully, slow → slowly.
Special cases:
• good → well (not goodly)
• fast → fast (not fastly)
• hard → hard (not hardly - this is another word: “barely”)
• late → late (not lately - this is “lately”)
Place: usually after the verb/object: She speaks English well.
formation: She sings beautifully. He works hard. She drives fast.

examples.sentence: He explained it clearly.
She ran fast.
They worked hard all day.

pattern: Adverbs of frequency and their place in a sentence
title: Adverbs of frequency and their place in a sentence
shortExplanation: always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never - before the main verb
longExplanation:
Adverbs of frequency: always, usually, often, sometimes, occasionally, rarely, rarely, never.
Place in a sentence:
• Before the main verb: She always drinks tea.
• After the verb to be: He is always late.
• After the auxiliary verb: She has never been to Italy.
Also: every day/week, once a week, twice a month - at the end of the sentence.
formation: always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never - before the main verb

examples.sentence: I usually wake up at 7.
She is never late for work.
examples.translation: She is never late for work.

examples.sentence: They meet once a week.

title: Order of adjectives before nouns
shortExplanation: a lovely small old red Italian leather bag
longExplanation:
When several adjectives appear before a noun, a strict order is observed: Opinion → Size → Age → Shape → Color → Origin → Material → Purpose
(Opinion → Size → Age → Shape → Color → Origin → Material → Purpose)
Example: a small beautiful old square brown French wooden writing desk
formation: a lovely small old red Italian leather bag

examples.sentence: a lovely little old cottage
a big red Italian sports car

title: Present Perfect - form and meaning
shortExplanation: I have seen it. She has gone. They have arrived.
longExplanation:
Present Perfect = have/has + V3 (third form of the verb).
Three main meanings:
1. Life Experience (no time specified): I have visited Tokyo.
2. Result in the present: I have lost my keys. (there are no keys now)
3. Unfinished action, ongoing now: She has lived here for 5 years.
V3 regular verbs = Past Simple (worked, played). Incorrect ones need to be known separately.
formation: I have seen it. She has gone. They have arrived.

examples.sentence: Have you ever eaten sushi?
I've just finished my homework.
She hasn't called yet.

title: ever / never / already / yet / just - Present Perfect markers
shortExplanation: Have you ever...? I've never... I've already... Not yet. I've just...
longExplanation:
ever - someday (in questions about experience). Location: in front of V3.
never - never (negative value). Location: in front of V3.
already - already (earlier than expected). Place: before V3 or at the end.
yet - already/yet. In questions (Have you finished yet?) and negations (I haven't finished yet). Place: end of sentence.
just - just now. Location: in front of V3.
formation: Have you ever...? I've never... I've already... Not yet. I've just...

examples.sentence: Have you ever been to Scotland?
I've never eaten snails.
I've already seen that film.

title: Present Perfect vs Past Simple - the key difference
shortExplanation: I've been to Paris (experience) vs I went to Paris in 2019 (specific time)
longExplanation:
This is one of the most important differences in English grammar.
Present Perfect - connection with the present, time is NOT indicated:
I've lost my wallet. (no wallet now - this is important)
Past Simple - completed past, time is indicated or implied:
I lost my wallet yesterday. (yesterday is a specific time)
formation: I've been to Paris (experience) vs I went to Paris in 2019 (specific time)

examples.sentence: I've met the new director. (он сейчас здесь, это актуально)
I met him last Tuesday. (конкретное время)

pattern: Present Perfect with for and since
title: Present Perfect with for and since
shortExplanation: I've lived here for 5 years / since 2019.
longExplanation:
for - duration: for two days, for a year, for a long time, for ages
since - starting point: since Monday, since I was a child, since 2015
The question “How long?” — How long + Present Perfect: How long have you known her?
formation: I've lived here for 5 years / since 2019.

examples.sentence: She's worked here for ten years.
examples.translation: She's been working here for ten years.

examples.sentence: I've known him since university.

title: Present Perfect Continuous: have been + V-ing
shortExplanation: I have been waiting for an hour. She has been studying all day.
longExplanation:
Present Perfect Continuous = have/has been + V-ing
Emphasis on duration or incompleteness of action. Answers the question “How long?”
Often explains the visible result in the present: You look tired - have you been running?
Difference with Present Perfect Simple:
• I've read 50 pages. - result, completeness
• I've been reading all evening. - emphasis on the process
formation: I have been waiting for an hour. She has been studying all day.

examples.sentence: I've been learning English for two years.
examples.translation: I've been learning English for two years now.

examples.sentence: Why are your hands dirty? — I've been fixing the car.
examples.translation: Why are your hands dirty? — I was repairing the car.

title: Past Continuous: was/were + V-ing
shortExplanation: I was reading at 8pm. They were talking all evening.
longExplanation:
Past Continuous = was/were + V-ing
Values:
1. Action in process at a specific moment in the past: At 9pm I was having dinner.
2. Background activity interrupted by another: I was walking when it started to rain.
3. Parallel actions: While she was cooking, he was watching TV.
formation: I was reading at 8pm. They were talking all evening.

examples.sentence: It was raining when I left home.
examples.translation: It was raining when I left the house.

examples.sentence: What were you doing at 7 yesterday?
examples.translation: What were you doing yesterday at 7?

title: Past Simple vs Past Continuous - background and event
shortExplanation: While I was cooking, he called. I was walking when it started to rain.
longExplanation:
Typical design: long background action (Past Continuous) + short event (Past Simple).
Unions:
• when - used with the Past Simple for the event: She was sleeping when the alarm went off.
• while/as - used with Past Continuous for background: While I was watching TV, the power went out.
formation: While I was cooking, he called. I was walking when it started to rain.

examples.sentence: She was having a bath when the phone rang.
examples.translation: She was taking a bath when the phone rang.

examples.sentence: While he was giving his speech, someone fell asleep.
examples.translation: While he was making his speech, someone fell asleep.

title: Type 0: If + Present, Present - facts and laws
shortExplanation: If you heat water to 100°C, it boils.
longExplanation:
Type zero - for scientific facts, laws of nature, general truths. Both actions always happen together.
Form: If + Present Simple, Present Simple
Instead of if you can use when: When you mix red and blue, you get purple.
formation: If you heat water to 100°C, it boils.

examples.sentence: If you heat ice, it melts.
examples.translation: If you heat ice, it melts.

examples.sentence: If it rains, the streets get wet.
examples.translation: If it rains, the streets get wet.

title: 1st type: If + Present Simple, will - real future
shortExplanation: If it rains tomorrow, I'll stay home.
longExplanation:
A real, probable situation in the future.
Form: If + Present Simple, will + infinitive
Instead of will in the main part you can: can, may, might, should.
Parts can be changed: I'll stay home if it rains. (without comma)
formation: If it rains tomorrow, I'll stay home.

examples.sentence: If she studies hard, she'll pass the exam.
examples.translation: If she studies well, she will pass the exam.

examples.sentence: If you need help, I can come.
examples.translation: If you need help, I can come.

title: Type 2: If + Past Simple, would - unreal present
shortExplanation: If I had a car, I would drive to work. If I were you...
longExplanation:
An unreal or unlikely situation in the present or future.
Form: If + Past Simple, would + infinitive
formation: If I had a car, I would drive to work. If I were you...

examples.sentence: If I won the lottery, I would travel the world.
examples.translation: If I won the lottery, I would travel the world.

examples.sentence: If I were taller, I'd play basketball.
examples.translation: If I were taller, I would play basketball.
